summary: In this Holy Week and Pascha special episode, the hosts Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick and Fr. Stephen De Young explore the theme of Christ's descent into Hades (the Harrowing of Hell) by examining ancient Near Eastern mythology, particularly the Ugaritic Baal Cycle, and its connections to biblical texts and Orthodox liturgical practices. They begin by discussing the ancient city of Ugarit and the discovery of the Baal Cycle, which provides insight into the Canaanite religion that Israel contended with. They then analyze Psalm 24 (23 LXX), showing how it directly responds to the Baal Cycle, asserting Yahweh's sovereignty over the cosmos and prophesying His victory over death and Hades. The episode also covers the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15), interpreting the crossing of the Red Sea as a battle against Egyptian gods, and connects it to baptism and the Paschal mystery. In the third half, they delve into Hosea 13:14, identifying the Canaanite deities Moth (Death), Sheol, Deber (Pestilence), and Keteb (Plague), and how God disarms them, as reflected in 1 Corinthians 15:55 and the Paschal troparion. The episode concludes with a reading from the Gospel of Nicodemus, depicting the dramatic dialogue between Hell and Satan as Christ arrives to liberate the righteous.

entities.title: Baal
entities.summary: A Canaanite storm god, son of El, whose worship was a constant temptation for Israel. The Baal Cycle describes his rebellion and descent into the underworld.

entities.title: Ugarit
entities.summary: An ancient city in northwestern Syria, destroyed around 1180 BC, whose clay tablets contained the Baal Cycle and other texts that illuminate biblical language and religion.

entities.title: Yam and Nahar
entities.summary: Canaanite gods of the sea and river, representing chaos, whom Baal overthrows. They are referenced in Psalm 24 as subdued by Yahweh.

entities.title: Moth (Mot)
entities.summary: The Canaanite god of death, who battles Baal and is taunted by Yahweh in Hosea 13:14. He is identified with Thanatos in Greek.

entities.title: Sheol
entities.summary: The Hebrew underworld, a place of the dead, often personified as a devouring creature. It is equivalent to Hades.

entities.title: Deber and Keteb
entities.summary: Canaanite gods of pestilence and plague, servants of Moth. They appear in Psalm 91 and Hosea 13, and are disarmed by God.

entities.title: Pharaoh
entities.summary: The king of Egypt in the Exodus narrative, whose army is drowned in the Sea of Reeds. He is depicted as a giant in Orthodox hymnography.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The incarnate Son of God, whose descent into Hades is the central theme of the episode, defeating death and liberating the righteous.

concepts.title: Harrowing of Hell
concepts.summary: The doctrine and event of Christ descending into Hades after His crucifixion to liberate the righteous dead, breaking the gates of death and defeating the devil.

concepts.title: Baal Cycle
concepts.summary: A collection of Ugaritic texts describing the mythological exploits of the god Baal, including his rebellion, victories, and descent into the underworld, which serves as a backdrop for biblical polemics.

concepts.title: Sacred Geography
concepts.summary: The concept that material places have spiritual significance and that events in the Bible occur in a landscape that overlaps with the unseen realm, such as the underworld and paradise.

concepts.title: Divine Smack Talk
concepts.summary: The rhetorical strategy in Scripture where Yahweh taunts pagan gods, asserting His superiority and reclaiming their attributes and powers.

concepts.title: Tradition Preserving Original Context
concepts.summary: The idea that Orthodox liturgical tradition has preserved the original ancient context of biblical texts, even when the historical background was lost, as seen in the use of Psalm 24 in the Paschal vigil.

claims.text: Psalm 24 is a direct response to the Baal Cycle, asserting that Yahweh, not Baal, is the true conqueror of chaos and the King of Glory who will invade Hades.
Christ's burial and descent into Hades is a biblical reality, and the Paschal liturgy re-presents this event, with the church doors symbolizing the gates of Hades.
The crossing of the Red Sea is depicted in Exodus 15 as a battle where Yahweh defeats the Egyptian gods, particularly through His right arm, which is a polemic against the god Montu.
Hosea 13:14 taunts the Canaanite gods Moth and Sheol, asking where their plagues (Deber and Keteb) are, indicating that God has disarmed death and taken away its weapons.
The Orthodox Church's liturgical tradition has preserved the original ancient context of biblical passages, such as Psalm 24, even when the historical background was lost for millennia.

scriptural_links.summary: The psalm is interpreted as a polemic against the Baal Cycle, declaring Yahweh's ownership of the earth, His conquest of chaos, and His entry into Hades as King of Glory.
The Song of the Sea is seen as a battle hymn celebrating Yahweh's victory over Pharaoh and the Egyptian gods, with the crossing of the sea as a passage through death to life.
The verse is a taunt against Moth and Sheol, asking where their plagues are, and is quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:55 to declare Christ's victory over death.
Paul quotes Hosea 13:14 to proclaim the defeat of death and Hades, connecting it to the resurrection and the disarming of demonic powers.
The psalm mentions Deber and Keteb, which are identified as Canaanite gods of plague and pestilence, and is used as an exorcism psalm in Orthodox tradition.

glossary.definition: Hebrew for 'Sea of Reeds', the body of water crossed by Israel, which also has a spiritual counterpart in Egyptian mythology as the sea of death.
A Canaanite god of pestilence, often translated as 'pestilence' in English Bibles, but recognized as a proper name in ancient context.
A Canaanite god of plague, often translated as 'plague' or 'destruction', but recognized as a proper name in ancient context.
Greek personification of death, used in the New Testament to refer to the power of death, often identified with the Canaanite god Moth.
Greek term for the underworld, equivalent to Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead, which Christ invaded and despoiled.
